boat.

fleet auxiliary tanker Dingle-

ping-up operations after last weeks
devastating snowstorm, a few words of
commentator are due, the linemen,
tree cutters and other employees of the
electric power and telephone companies
for their efforts to restore services for
beleaguered customers throughout this
area. In some respects the wet snow
and wind gusts caused more trouble for
the utility crews than some Of the more
severe hurricanes. Not only were lines
broken by falling poles and trees, but
the heavy snow seriously handicapped
the repairmen. Repair trucks had diff
Guilty in reaching the scenes Of damage
and the workmen then had to wade
through knee-deep snowfalls to cut
dangling hot wires and string new ones.


The crews, reinforced by workmen
summoned from distant areas that had
escaped the brunt of the storm, labored
around the clock-some Of them missing
meals and sleep in the process. Grad
ually, however, light, heat and commu-
nications we're restored and households
and businesses resumed normal opera
tions. \ was an extraordinarily bard
Job welF done. ~

When an F-10O-F Jet trainer COL

Senger plane over Las Vegas last month,
killing 40 people, an Air Force spokes-
man said the jet was following normal"
flight procedures. Apparently this
spokesman was correct, up to point.
The flight procedures were indeed nor
mal-and needlesSly hazardous.


This is the only conclusion which
can be drawn from testimony given a
House subcommittee concerning the COL
lision, and released by Representative
Preston, of Georgia


According to this testimony. the
jet, flying at $4,000 feet in clear weather.
received permission from Nellis Air
Force base to penetrate
for landing. At 81 900 feet it crashed
into the air liner. The liner, flying at its
designated altitude in the proper air
lane passed that same spot at approx
imately the same time every day. This
TACT was known to the Nellis base per-
sonnet. Why, then, was the Jet, whose
position must also have been known to
the base personnel, given permission to
descend at that particular time? And
why is it necessary, with all the air
space available over Nevada, to conduct
training exercises over an established
commercial air lane?


The answer can hardly be that
there was only remote chance of a
collision. For the testimony revealed
that there have been 1000 "near misses"
in the air during the past two years.
The term NEAR misses" may be some
thing less than precise. But there is
nothing imprecise about what happened
over Las Vegas. If there had been little
more care, little more attention to
reasonable safety requirements, the
40 victims would be alive today.

last April between commercial airliner
and jet fighter near Las Vegas, Nevada,

Board. This report reveals that it cost
40 lives to bring about precautionary
measures that might well have averted
the accident-meaSureS which, in view
of a number of near collisions preceding
the fatal crash, should have been taken
earlier.


The CAB has placed the blame for
conditions which made the accident pos
Sible on both the Air Force and the Civil
AeronauticS Administration. 1t found
that military jet training operations and
civil airliner flights had been danger
ously intermixed on the civil airway near
NelliS Air Force Base, that complaints
of ar-encounters with jet fighters had
been made by commercial airline pilots
and that nothing was done by military
or civil aviation officials to correct the
situation. That is. nothing was done
until United passenger craft with At
persons aboard and an Air Force jet
carrying two officers collided, sending
all to their deaths.


On the fatal day an Air Force train
ing jet was on an Air approved
fight course, the board said, where
most commercially air traffic could rea-
sonably be expected" The jets course
was within the airway path of the United
airliner. Just as the airliner approached
Las Vegas on scheduled course and time
and at approved altitude, the fighter
plane began a descent that brought it
into collision angle near the Nellis
base. The particular angle of approach
of the two aircraft, the CAB pointed out,
was one in which it was extremely diff
cult for either pilot to see the other
plane.

Britain's race riots have introduced

scarce jobs. A rise in degeneracy and
crime also has been reported. What
ever the reason or reasons, the race
question, almost unheard Of in the past

virulent form. Stern police measures,

lem from getting out of hand, but the

Following so closely upon the dis
closure that OIL NEAR misses" were
reported by aircraft last years. OF
them over Washington, Maryland and
Virginia-the latest air-collision tragedy
near Jefferson, Md, accentuates the
need for better trafiic control for the
Nations Always. The inexcusable crash
which cost IL lives yesterday occurred,
ironically, as Federal authorities we're
proposing TO Congress a billion-dollar
program for jet-age modernization of
the airways. The Maryland accident and
near-miss tabulation provide convincing
evidence of the urgent need for imme-
date action on this program.


There was a time when traffic con-
troll was considered necessary chiefly in
the vicinity of large airports. But as
commercial and military air flights have
increased and the speed and passenger
carrying characteristics of aircraft have
multiplied, dangerous congestion has
developed not only near the big cities
but on the principal air routes across
the continent. Control Of commercial
flights has been strengthened substan-
TALLY by the Civil Aeronautics Admins
tration in recent years, but military
aviation largely has been free to go
where it pleaseS, when it pleases. And
the number of near misses and Of actual
collisions between civil and military
planes has risen ominously. Yesterdays
collision between turbo-prop Viscount
airliner and a National Guard jet
trainer came only few weeks after
the Las Vegas airliner military Jet
catastrophe that took 40 lives. In both
cases the Jets apparently flew into the
civilian planes, although the latter were
on their prescribed courses.


In reporting to Congress the 1857
near-miss total, the Civil Aeronautics
Board stressed that many other close
calls may have occurred. Pilots, the
CAB said, have an inherent antipathy"
to filling out reports. But the reported
total was shocking enough in its impli-
cations of potential danger to warrant
prompt and effective action to bring
the airways under better control-for
military as we'll as civilian aircraft.
Many lives are at stake.

the symbol Of the larger life that q
woman with will can achieve.

Heavy fighting erupted today

showdown battle between gov

It was by far the worst battle

lion began in Lebanon So days

At least three big battles were

Intensive Firing


The most intensive firing was

palace. about 300 yards away.


Another big battle was being
fought about 300 yards in the
opposite direction. in the Mos
lem quarter of Basta, the bar
ricaded sector used as rebel
headquarters.


The third battle was raging

prison.


1t was not Immediately known
which side launched the attack.


But, with United Nations OBJ
servers moving into Lebanon, it

attempt to bring down the gov
eminent.


1t also could be a government
offensive to wipe out insurgents

Fighting on the outskirts of

gents tried to capture Ramel

the city and the airport. First

fought their way into the
prison yard. But before they

security forces attacked and
were reported driving them
away.

homes and buildings. Motorists

and took shelter.


In banning the opposition

mining the security of this East
